title: Days until warmer
statement:
A weather station logs one temperature per day in `temps`.

For each day, return how many days you would wait until a strictly warmer day. If no warmer day comes later, use 0 for that day.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does an equal temperature count as warmer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, it must be strictly warmer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no warmer day comes?
How many days?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Rules out scanning forward from every day.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What range are temperatures in?
clarifyingQuestions.why: A small range allows a different approach, but the stack works regardless.

edgeCases.why: Equal temperatures are not warmer: all zeros.
Nothing warmer ever: all zeros, and the stack fills up.
One warm day resolves many waiting days at once.

approaches.name: Scan forward from each day
approaches.idea: For each day, look ahead until a warmer day.
approaches.tradeoffs: Quadratic when temperatures fall for a long time.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack of waiting days
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of positions still waiting for a warmer day; their temperatures decrease from bottom to top. Each new day pops every waiting day that is colder and fills in its answer.
approaches.tradeoffs: Each day is pushed and popped at most once.

optimal.name: Monotonic decreasing stack
optimal.explanation: Initialize answers to 0. For each day i, while the stack is non-empty and the temperature at its top is lower than temps[i], pop j and set answer[j] = i - j. Then push i. Days left on the stack never found a warmer day and keep 0.

hintLadder: Which earlier days could today be the answer for?
Among days still waiting, what do you know about their temperatures?
What structure lets you resolve the most recent waiting days first?
Keep a stack of indexes with decreasing temperatures; pop while today is warmer.

expectedMentions.what: Asks whether equal temperatures count as warmer
Proposes a stack of waiting days with decreasing temperatures
Explains why it is O(n): each index is pushed and popped once
Explains storing indexes rather than temperatures to compute the wait
Traces an example showing several pops at once

followUps: Return the next warmer temperature instead of the wait.
The list is circular: after the last day, wrap around to the first.

walkthrough.say: Warmer means strictly warmer, so an equal temperature doesn’t count? And days with no warmer day get zero?
Brute force scans forward from each day until it finds something warmer. If temperatures keep falling, that’s n squared.

Instead, think about days that are still waiting. If I keep them on a stack, their temperatures must be decreasing from bottom to top, because a warmer day would have resolved the colder ones below it. When a new day comes, I pop every waiting day that’s colder and record the gap. Each day is pushed and popped once, so it’s O(n).
I store indexes on the stack, because I need the positions to compute the wait.

For 18, 16, 17, 21, 19, 15, 20: 18 and 16 wait. 17 resolves 16 with a gap of 1, then waits on top of 18. 21 resolves 17 and 18, giving 1 and 3. 19 and 15 wait, then 20 resolves 15 and 19 with 1 and 2. 21 and 20 stay at 0. That matches.
Equal temperatures: the comparison is strictly less than, so 20, 20, 20 never pops and all stay zero.
O(n) time, O(n) space for the stack in the worst case of falling temperatures.
